cards.explanation: The answer is that Paul opposes him to his face. Paul says, "…I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned." (Galatians 2:11) To his face means Paul took it up with Cephas directly. I once avoided a hard talk for a whole week, friends, and my mustache got tired just from the dodging.

The answer is the Gentiles. Verse 12 says that before certain men came from James, Cephas "…used to eat with the Gentiles." (Galatians 2:12) Gentiles are people who aren't Jews. A shared table says a lot, and Cephas was sitting right at it.

The answer is that he's afraid of the circumcision group. The text says he drew back and separated himself "…for fear of those in the circumcision group." (Galatians 2:12) Fear changed where he sat. I think we've all picked a seat because of who was watching.
The word is hypocrisy. Paul says, "The other Jews joined him in his hypocrisy…" (Galatians 2:13) He doesn't soften it, friends. Sometimes a hard word is the kind thing to say out loud.

The answer is True. The text says that "…by their hypocrisy even Barnabas was led astray." (Galatians 2:13) Barnabas had gone up to Jerusalem with Paul (Galatians 2:1), so I think that one stings. It shows how strong the pull of a crowd can be.
The answer is False. Paul says he spoke to Cephas "…in front of them all…" (Galatians 2:14) Nobody got pulled aside, friends. I think it was a very quiet room for a very loud sentence.

The answer is that he pressures Gentiles to live like Jews. Paul asks, "…how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?" (Galatians 2:14) Cephas was living like a Gentile himself, so the pressure didn't match his own life. Paul points at that gap.

The answer is by faith in Jesus Christ. Paul says "…a man is not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ." (Galatians 2:16) Justified means made right with God. It isn't earned, it's trusted. Write that one on your oven door, bakers.

The answer is True. Paul says, "So we, too, have believed in Christ Jesus…" (Galatians 2:16) Paul counts himself in that "we," right alongside the Jews by birth he's speaking about. Nobody gets a side door.
The answer is "Certainly not." Paul asks if Christ is a minister of sin, and he says, "Certainly not!" (Galatians 2:17) He doesn't pause or hedge, friends. Just a flat no.

The word is lawbreaker. Paul says, "If I rebuild what I have already torn down, I prove myself to be a lawbreaker." (Galatians 2:18) Building it back up is the very thing that trips him. Tear it down, then leave it down.

The answer is True. Paul writes, "For through the law I died to the law so that I might live to God." (Galatians 2:19) It sounds upside down, but the goal is clear: living to God. I still had to read it twice.
The answer is Christ. Paul says, "I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me." (Galatians 2:20) It's about as personal as a sentence gets, friends.

The answer is that he loved Paul and gave Himself up for him. Paul says he lives by faith in the Son of God, "…who loved me and gave Himself up for me." (Galatians 2:20) Notice the "me." He says it so personally that I always want to read it slowly.

The answer is False. Paul says, "…if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing." (Galatians 2:21) He says it right after "I do not set aside the grace of God." That's why he holds onto grace, friends.
